questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy can hop on one foot, copy a cross, dress without help and tell a connected story. His development is:
options: Appropriate for age across gross motor, fine motor, language and social domains
questions.concept: Copying a cross and hopping belong to 4 years, copying a square and a triangle to 4.5 and 5 years, and using a spoon well and pulling off shoes to 2 years, so mapping each skill to its domain and age is how delay is identified.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Growth and Development

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A term infant's weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 3rd centile over 4 months while length and head circumference remain on the 50th. This pattern indicates:
options: Wasting from inadequate calorie intake or increased losses, the earliest anthropometric change in undernutrition
questions.concept: Weight falls first, then length (stunting) and only late does head circumference fall, so the sequence of centile crossing distinguishes acute undernutrition from an endocrine or genetic cause.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Growth and Development

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child presents at 9 months having received only BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B at birth. The correct approach is:
options: Give all due vaccines simultaneously at separate sites and complete the schedule without restarting
Restart the whole schedule from the beginning
Give one vaccine per visit at monthly intervals
Defer until the child is 1 year old
questions.concept: There is no maximum interval between doses, so a lapsed schedule is resumed rather than restarted, and simultaneous administration at separate sites is safe and improves coverage.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated in a child with symptomatic HIV and severe immunosuppression?
options: BCG and other live vaccines such as oral polio and measles-containing vaccine in severe immunosuppression
questions.concept: Live vaccines risk disseminated vaccine-strain disease, notably BCG-osis, whereas inactivated vaccines are safe and indeed particularly important in immunodeficient children.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 5-year-old sustains a clean minor wound and has received all five doses of DPT and DT as scheduled. The tetanus prophylaxis required is:
options: None, as the primary course plus boosters gives adequate protection for a clean minor wound
questions.concept: Fully immunised children need no additional dose for a clean minor wound, whereas a dirty or deep wound needs a booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which is the correct site and route for BCG vaccine in a newborn?
options: Intradermal into the left upper arm over the deltoid insertion
questions.concept: The intradermal route produces the papule, ulcer and scar sequence over 6 to 12 weeks, and injecting too deeply causes an abscess rather than the intended local reaction.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which condition is a true contraindication to further doses of pertussis-containing vaccine?
options: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose, or encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose
Fever of 39 degrees after the last dose
Persistent crying for 2 hours after the last dose
questions.concept: Most reactions once considered contraindications, including prolonged crying, high fever and febrile seizures, are now regarded as precautions only, so unnecessary withholding of pertussis vaccine is a common error.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which statement about the vitamin A supplementation schedule under the national programme is correct?
options: The first dose of 100000 IU is given at 9 months with measles-rubella vaccine, then 200000 IU every 6 months up to 5 years
A single dose is given at birth only
It is given monthly throughout infancy
It is given only to children with xerophthalmia
questions.concept: Nine biannual megadoses reduce all-cause child mortality by improving epithelial integrity and immune function, and giving it with measles vaccine improves coverage.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which finding after measles vaccination in a well-nourished child is expected and requires only reassurance?
options: Mild fever with a transient rash 5 to 12 days later
questions.concept: The live attenuated virus replicates over about a week, so any fever or rash appears in that window; immediate reactions suggest hypersensitivity to a vaccine component rather than vaccine viraemia.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which vaccine must never be frozen, and why?
options: Adsorbed vaccines such as DPT, hepatitis B and pentavalent, because freezing damages the aluminium adjuvant and destroys potency
Oral polio vaccine, because freezing inactivates it
Measles vaccine, because freezing causes reversion
BCG, because freezing kills the bacilli
questions.concept: The shake test detects a frozen adsorbed vaccine, whereas live vaccines such as oral polio and measles tolerate freezing and are stored in the deep freezer, which is why ice packs are conditioned before use.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Why does the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine need to be given within 24 hours?
options: Perinatal transmission occurs mainly at delivery, and immunisation within 24 hours prevents the 90 percent chronicity risk of neonatal infection
The vaccine is ineffective after 24 hours at any age
It reduces the number of subsequent doses needed
questions.concept: The younger the age at infection the higher the chronicity rate, so the timeliness of the birth dose, with immunoglobulin where available for infants of highly viraemic mothers, is a key hepatitis B control indicator.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which principle explains why oral polio vaccine contributes to herd protection more than inactivated polio vaccine?
options: It induces intestinal mucosal immunity and vaccine virus spreads to unimmunised contacts
questions.concept: Secretory IgA in the gut interrupts wild virus transmission and the shed vaccine virus immunises contacts, which is also the mechanism by which circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus arises in under-immunised populations.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which condition included in newborn screening causes irreversible intellectual disability if not treated within the first weeks of life?
questions.concept: Thyroid hormone is essential for myelination and cortical development in the first months, so screening at 48 to 72 hours with prompt levothyroxine prevents the cretinism that would otherwise follow.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which clinical clue should prompt urgent testing for an inborn error of metabolism in a previously well neonate?
options: Deterioration after a symptom-free interval with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis and a family history of neonatal death
A single episode of poor feeding
questions.concept: The characteristic pattern is a well baby who decompensates as feeding is established and the toxic metabolite accumulates, so first-line tests are glucose, blood gas, ammonia, lactate and urine ketones.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: A neonate with vomiting, hyperammonaemia and a respiratory alkalosis has an inborn error most likely affecting:
questions.concept: Ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre, so an early respiratory alkalosis with hyperammonaemia and no acidosis points to a urea cycle defect rather than an organic acidaemia, which causes acidosis with ketosis.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which chromosomal syndrome is most likely in an infant with hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, a flat nasal bridge and duodenal atresia?
questions.concept: The double bubble of duodenal atresia, atrioventricular septal defect and Hirschsprung disease are the classic structural associations, and the risk of transient myeloproliferative disorder and later leukaemia is increased.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which finding differentiates trisomy 18 from trisomy 13 in a newborn?
options: Clenched hands with overlapping index finger and rocker-bottom feet in trisomy 18, versus midline defects and polydactyly in trisomy 13
questions.concept: Trisomy 13 features holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia and postaxial polydactyly, whereas trisomy 18 features the characteristic hand posture, small chin and short sternum.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which metabolic disorder is suggested by a positive urinary reducing substance test with a negative glucose oxidase dipstick and cataracts in an infant?
questions.concept: Galactose is a reducing sugar not detected by the glucose-specific strip, and galactitol accumulation causes cataract; Escherichia coli sepsis is a classic accompanying presentation and a lactose-free diet is life-saving.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which sample and timing are used for newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry?
options: Heel-prick dried blood spot taken after 24 hours of feeding, ideally at 48 to 72 hours
questions.concept: Sampling before feeding is established gives false negatives for disorders that require substrate accumulation, and sampling too early gives false positives for congenital hypothyroidism because of the physiological TSH surge.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: A child with coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness and normal intelligence has which class of disorder?
options: Mucopolysaccharidosis, likely Hurler-Scheie or Scheie type
questions.concept: Urinary glycosaminoglycan screening followed by enzyme assay identifies the type, and preserved intelligence with corneal clouding distinguishes the attenuated forms from Hurler disease and from Hunter disease, which spares the cornea.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Why does a child with phenylketonuria on a strict low-phenylalanine diet still require tyrosine supplementation?
options: Tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid because it can no longer be made from phenylalanine
questions.concept: The blocked hydroxylation step removes the sole endogenous source of tyrosine, which is the precursor of dopamine, noradrenaline, thyroxine and melanin, explaining the fair hair and pale skin of untreated disease.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Inborn errors, newborn screening & chromosomal syndromes
questions.stem: Which principle governs the acute management of a metabolic crisis in a suspected inborn error before the diagnosis is known?
options: Stop protein intake, give high-dose intravenous dextrose to halt catabolism, and treat hyperammonaemia while awaiting results
Give a high-protein feed to correct deficiency
questions.concept: Reversing catabolism removes the substrate driving toxin accumulation, and specific measures such as sodium benzoate, carnitine or vitamin cofactors are added as the pathway is identified, with dialysis for severe hyperammonaemia.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Inborn Errors of Metabolism and Genetics

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is always pathological and most often indicates:
options: Haemolysis from Rh or ABO incompatibility, or G6PD deficiency
questions.concept: Physiological jaundice never appears before 24 hours, so early onset demands immediate measurement of bilirubin with blood group, direct Coombs test, haematocrit and reticulocyte count.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Neonatology

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes breast milk jaundice from breastfeeding failure jaundice?
options: Breast milk jaundice appears in the second week in a thriving baby, whereas failure jaundice appears in the first week with weight loss and dehydration
Breast milk jaundice causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
questions.concept: The distinction matters because the treatment of breastfeeding failure is to support and increase feeding, whereas breast milk jaundice is benign and breastfeeding is continued.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Neonatology

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Prolonged jaundice beyond 2 weeks with pale stools, dark urine and a raised conjugated bilirubin requires urgent evaluation for:
options: Biliary atresia, because the Kasai portoenterostomy is most successful before 8 weeks of age
questions.concept: Any conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant is pathological, and delay past 8 to 10 weeks sharply reduces the success of surgical drainage and the chance of avoiding transplantation.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Neonatology

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, which action is taken if the heart rate remains below 100 after 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilation?
options: Check and correct ventilation technique using the corrective steps, then continue ventilation
questions.concept: Ventilation is the cornerstone of neonatal resuscitation because the problem is almost always respiratory, and compressions are started only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Neonatology

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which finding in a neonate with sepsis carries the highest mortality and requires the most urgent intervention?
options: Shock with poor perfusion, prolonged capillary refill and metabolic acidosis
questions.concept: Neonatal septic shock progresses rapidly, so antibiotics within the first hour with careful volume expansion and inotropic support determine outcome, and the commonest early organisms are group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Neonatology

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Low birth weight is defined as a birth weight below:
questions.concept: Very low birth weight is below 1500 g and extremely low birth weight below 1000 g, and a low birth weight baby may be preterm, small for gestational age, or both.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which method reduces mortality in stable low birth weight infants and can be provided in low-resource settings?
options: Kangaroo mother care with continuous skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breastfeeding
questions.concept: Skin-to-skin contact stabilises temperature, heart rate and breathing, promotes breastfeeding and reduces infection and mortality, and it can begin as soon as the baby is haemodynamically stable.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which score is used to estimate gestational age from physical and neuromuscular maturity in a newborn?
questions.concept: The Apgar score assesses transition at birth, and the Silverman-Andersen and Downes scores grade respiratory distress, so each score answers a different question.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which complication is a preterm infant of 28 weeks most at risk of in the first 72 hours?
options: Intraventricular haemorrhage from the fragile germinal matrix
questions.concept: The subependymal germinal matrix is highly vascular with poor autoregulation, so fluctuations in pressure and carbon dioxide in the first days cause bleeding, whereas the other complications develop over weeks.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Screening for retinopathy of prematurity is indicated in which infants, and when?
options: Infants below 34 weeks or 1750 g, or those who received oxygen, screened from 3 to 4 weeks of age
questions.concept: Timely screening allows laser or anti-VEGF treatment at the threshold stage, and both hyperoxia and fluctuating oxygen saturations contribute, which is why saturation targets are set carefully.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which feature suggests a small for gestational age infant is asymmetrically growth restricted rather than constitutionally small?
options: Reduced weight with relatively preserved length and head circumference and a raised ponderal index deficit
questions.concept: Asymmetrical restriction indicates late uteroplacental insufficiency with brain sparing, and these infants are at particular risk of hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia and hypothermia after birth.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which measure best prevents hypothermia in a preterm infant immediately after delivery?
options: Delivery room temperature of 25 to 28 degrees with immediate drying, a pre-warmed radiant warmer, cap and plastic wrap
Delayed drying to allow vernix absorption
questions.concept: Heat is lost by evaporation, conduction, convection and radiation, and preterm infants have a high surface-area-to-mass ratio with little brown fat, so the warm chain must begin in the delivery room.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Why is a preterm infant at greater risk of necrotising enterocolitis than a term infant?
options: Immature gut motility, barrier function and immunity with abnormal bacterial colonisation, aggravated by rapid feed advancement and formula
questions.concept: Exclusive human milk, standardised slow feed advancement and avoiding prolonged empirical antibiotics reduce risk, and pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal radiograph is the diagnostic hallmark.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Newborn assessment, prematurity & low birth weight
questions.stem: Which physiological feature explains why a preterm infant develops apnoea of prematurity?
options: Immature central chemoreceptor response with a paradoxical ventilatory response to hypoxia and an immature Hering-Breuer reflex
questions.concept: Caffeine acts on adenosine receptors to raise central respiratory drive and reduces the frequency of apnoea and the need for ventilation, which is why it is standard in very preterm infants.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Care of the Newborn

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 6-week-old male has projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds with visible peristalsis and a palpable olive-shaped epigastric mass. The expected metabolic abnormality is:
options: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.concept: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid drives the alkalosis, and as potassium is depleted the kidney exchanges hydrogen rather than potassium for sodium, producing acid urine despite systemic alkalosis; correction precedes pyloromyotomy.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 9-month-old has intermittent severe colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, a sausage-shaped abdominal mass and redcurrant jelly stools. The initial management is:
options: Resuscitation followed by air or hydrostatic reduction under imaging guidance
questions.concept: Non-operative reduction succeeds in most cases of ileocolic intussusception, and surgery is reserved for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction; a pathological lead point is more likely beyond 2 years.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which feature suggests coeliac disease in a child with chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive?
options: Positive tissue transglutaminase IgA with a raised total IgA, confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy
questions.concept: Serology must be taken while the child is on a gluten-containing diet, total IgA is measured because deficiency causes false negatives, and biopsy shows crypt hyperplasia with intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes Hirschsprung disease from functional constipation in an infant?
options: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours with an empty rectum on examination and explosive stool on withdrawal of the finger
questions.concept: Aganglionosis causes failure of the rectosphincteric reflex, so anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks confirm it.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate has bilious vomiting on day 2 with a double bubble on abdominal radiograph and no distal gas. The likely diagnosis and association are:
options: Duodenal atresia, associated with Down syndrome
Malrotation with volvulus, associated with situs inversus
Jejunal atresia, associated with cystic fibrosis
questions.concept: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is always pathological, and the absence of distal gas distinguishes complete atresia from stenosis or malrotation, which requires urgent contrast study because volvulus threatens the whole midgut.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which is the commonest cause of chronic liver disease in Indian children and is screened for by which test?
options: Wilson disease, screened by serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, screened by protein electrophoresis
Autoimmune hepatitis, screened by ANA alone
questions.concept: Wilson disease is treatable and easily missed, so ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings and sometimes liver copper estimation are performed in any child with unexplained liver disease.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 3-year-old has recurrent painless rectal bleeding, and a technetium pertechnetate scan shows uptake in the right lower quadrant. The diagnosis is:
options: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
questions.concept: The rule of twos describes the diverticulum, and the scan localises ectopic gastric mucosa whose acid secretion ulcerates adjacent ileal mucosa, causing the bleeding.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which pattern of liver function tests suggests neonatal cholestasis rather than physiological jaundice, and what is the immediate imperative?
options: A conjugated fraction above 20 percent of total bilirubin with pale stools, requiring urgent evaluation for biliary atresia
Normal bilirubin with a raised alkaline phosphatase
questions.concept: Stool colour cards and early measurement of the conjugated fraction are the practical screening tools, because the window for a successful Kasai procedure closes within the first two months.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Why is fat-soluble vitamin supplementation essential in a child with chronic cholestasis?
options: Reduced bile salt delivery to the intestine impairs micelle formation, so absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K fails
Vitamin absorption is normal but utilisation is impaired
questions.concept: Deficiency causes night blindness, rickets, neuropathy and coagulopathy respectively, so water-miscible preparations at high dose with monitoring of levels and prothrombin time are needed.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders
